title: Swedish Housing Law — Chapter 12 Core Expansion
purpose: Expand the bounded Swedish Housing Law Logical Universe with second-hand letting, forfeiture and recovery, extension/security-of-tenure, rent review and repayment paths. Open-textured standards remain assessment questions rather than fabricated deterministic outcomes.

sources.title: Prop. 2025/26:187 En mer flexibel hyresmarknad
sources.note: Interpretive background to the 2026 private-letting reform and related Chapter 12 amendments; not installed as a statutory rule.

sections.summary: A tenant may not let or otherwise grant the apartment to another for independent use without landlord consent, subject to statutory exceptions and permission under section 40.

The Housing and Tenancy Tribunal may permit second-hand letting when the tenant has considerable reasons, the landlord lacks justified reason to refuse, and residential second-hand rent does not exceed the statutory reasonable-rent ceiling.

A tenant may not accommodate outsiders to an extent the landlord should not reasonably have to accept; size, duration, living conditions, management burden and disturbance risk are expressly relevant assessment factors.

Chapter 12 lists grounds on which the tenancy can be forfeited, including residential rent delay over one week, unauthorized second-hand letting without valid excuse, unreasonable second-hand rent without valid excuse, and specified misuse or serious breaches.
For several forfeiture grounds timely rectification before termination prevents eviction on that ground; other grounds are subject to knowledge and termination time limits.

A residential tenant whose tenancy was forfeited for late rent may recover the tenancy by paying within the statutory three-week recovery period after the required notice and social-welfare notification conditions are met.
Waiver of the residential tenant's extension right must satisfy statutory form and, in many situations, tribunal-approval requirements; specified limited situations are exempt from approval.

A residential tenant generally has a right to extension after landlord termination unless one of the statutory exceptions applies; several exceptions expressly require reasonableness or interest balancing.
A landlord termination is ineffective in an extension dispute unless the dispute is referred to the Housing and Tenancy Tribunal within the statutory time, unless the tenant has already moved.
When the extension question is unresolved at the end of the term, the tenant generally has a right to remain until the question is finally decided, subject to the statutory enforcement exception.
Sections 54–55 e on residential rent and terms apply subject to exceptions including certain short-duration furnished or holiday lettings and a unit forming part of the lessor's own home.
A party seeking a change in rent or other terms must notify the counterparty in writing and may apply to the Housing and Tenancy Tribunal if agreement is not reached.

Disputed rent is set at a reasonable amount; it is not reasonable if markedly higher than equivalent apartments by use value. For second-hand residential letting, rent above the first-hand rent plus bounded additions is never reasonable.

For rooms and specified second-hand residential lets, the tribunal can order repayment of rent received above the statutory reasonable amount, with the statutory retrospective limit and interest rules.

The proposition describes the 2026 reform as creating a clearer private-letting regime, more flexible letting, revised second-hand boundaries and related Chapter 12 changes. It is interpretive material, not statutory truth.

rules.explanation: Under Chapter 12 section 39, independent second-hand use requires landlord consent unless a statutory exception or tribunal permission applies.
The represented facts satisfy the modeled statutory criteria for tribunal permission: considerable reason, no justified landlord refusal and reasonable residential second-hand rent.
A permission request opens a multi-factor statutory assessment; the robot does not infer missing reasons, landlord objections or rent reasonableness.
Section 41 is intentionally represented as an assessment zone: several listed circumstances must be weighed before the extent of outsider accommodation can be judged unreasonable.
For a residential tenancy, more than one week of rent delay is a statutory forfeiture ground, but the separate recovery mechanism in section 44 must still be considered.
The represented facts include landlord termination for rent delay and payment within the three-week statutory recovery period after notice, so the modeled section 44 recovery path is activated.

Unauthorized residential second-hand letting without required consent/permission and without valid excuse is a statutory forfeiture ground, while the minor-significance safeguard and section 43 timing rules remain separate checks.
Where the represented section 41 misuse is corrected before landlord termination, section 43 prevents eviction on that modeled ground.
For represented residential second-hand letting, rent above the first-hand rent plus permitted additions is never reasonable; repayment scope still depends on amount, period and application facts.
Chapter 12 section 46 starts from a residential tenant extension right after landlord termination, subject to listed exceptions.
A serious tenant breach can defeat extension only after the statutory degree/reasonableness assessment; this is deliberately not collapsed into a binary rule.
Major renovation is not an automatic loss of tenancy; necessity, practical ability to remain and reasonableness toward the tenant must be assessed.
For the represented one-/two-family non-business situation, the landlord's disposal interest must be balanced against whether the tenant should reasonably move.
Section 50 generally allows the tenant to remain until the extension question is finally decided when the dispute is still pending at term end.
A Chapter 12 residential rent-change dispute follows the written notice and tribunal application route in section 54, subject to the statutory scope rules.
